## Summary

There is no direct mismatch between `src/comm.m` and `src/test.cpp` for the simple handshake they are trying to use.

### What each file is meant to do

- `src/comm.m`
  - Opens the serial port on COM3 at 115200.
  - Sends one byte: `S`
  - That is basically a “start” signal to the Arduino.
  - Then closes the port.

- `src/test.cpp`
  - Waits until it receives a byte from serial.
  - If it sees `S`, it sets `initialized = true`
  - Then it toggles the onboard LED every 500 microseconds.
  - This is a simple Arduino “ready/start” test.

So the intended handshake is:
1. MATLAB sends `S`
2. Arduino receives `S`
3. Arduino starts running its autonomous loop

---

## Are there errors?

### Likely real issues

- COM port mismatch:
  - `src/comm.m` uses COM3.
  - Your actual Arduino may be on a different port, like COM4, COM5, etc.

- The files are not the full characterization system:
  - `src/test.cpp` is only a basic LED test
  - `src/main.cpp` is the actual voltage-writing / analog-reading sketch for the MOSFET test
  - It writes DAC voltages and reads back ADC values, then prints them over serial

- `src/comm.m` does not read anything back from the Arduino:
  - It only sends the start command.
  - If you expect MATLAB to collect measurement data, this script is incomplete.

---

## Important distinction

If you want the simple startup test:
- Upload `src/test.cpp`
- Run `src/comm.m`

If you want the real MOSFET characterization:
- Upload `src/main.cpp`
- Then MATLAB needs a communication script that reads the serial output, not just sends `S`

So the answer is:

- Between `src/comm.m` and `src/test.cpp`: no direct protocol error
- Between the project intent and the actual scripts: yes, there is a mismatch in scope
- The quick test script and the real characterization script are different programs

> The biggest practical issue is likely the port name and the fact that `src/comm.m` is not designed to collect data from the board.

are these files going to communicate between each other?

_**Agent (copilot/auto)**_

I’m verifying the exact serial protocol between the MATLAB side and the Arduino side so I can answer whether they will actually exchange data.

## Yes — they are compatible for a simple start signal

If you upload `src/test.cpp` to the Arduino and run `src/comm.m`, they will communicate at the serial level, provided the COM port is correct and the Arduino is actually on that port.

### Why they match

- In `src/comm.m`, MATLAB sends:
  - `write(arduino, uint8('S'), "uint8");`
- In `src/test.cpp`, Arduino waits for serial data and checks:
  - `char command = Serial.read();`
  - `if (command == 'S')`

That is a valid match:
- MATLAB sends a single byte with value `S`
- Arduino reads that same byte and treats it as the start command

So the handshake is effectively:
1. MATLAB sends `S`
2. Arduino receives `S`
3. Arduino sets `initialized = true`
4. LED starts blinking

---

## Important limitation

This is only a one-way command, not a full data exchange.

- `src/comm.m` does not read any data back from the Arduino
- `src/test.cpp` does not send anything back to MATLAB
- MATLAB immediately does `clear arduino;` after sending the command

So the communication is “start signal only,” not “control + feedback.”

---

## Things that can still fail

- COM port mismatch:
  - `src/comm.m` uses `COM3`
  - Your board may be on another COM port
- Baud mismatch:
  - both use `115200`, so that part matches
- The Arduino must be uploaded with `src/test.cpp`, not the main sketch, if you are testing this exact protocol

---

## Final answer

Yes, these two files are designed to communicate with each other for the simple test case. The core protocol matches. The main caveat is that it is only a start command, not a full MATLAB-to-Arduino measurement protocol.

If you want, I can also show you the proper MATLAB code to read the actual measurement values that `src/main.cpp` prints back over serial.

That means the upload command did not complete successfully, but the actual text of the failure is not visible in the snippet you shared.

## Most likely cause in this project

Your board configuration in `platformio.ini` is:

If the board connected to your computer is not actually a Nano R4, or the port is wrong, PlatformIO will fail during upload. The common upload errors are:

- “No serial port found”
- “Failed to open serial port”
- “Board not found”
- “Upload protocol error”
- “No device found on COMx”

_**Agent (copilot/auto)**_

## Root cause

Your upload is failing because both Arduino source files define the same required functions:

- `src/main.cpp`
- `src/test.cpp`

Both contain:

- 
- 

PlatformIO compiles every `.cpp` file in the `src` folder, so it tries to link both at once and hits:

> `multiple definition of 'setup'`
>
> `multiple definition of 'loop'`

This is exactly the error shown in your terminal.

---

## Why this happens

In Arduino/PlatformIO, there must be only one  and one  in the active build.

If you have more than one file in `src` that defines them, the linker fails.

---

## Fix options

### Best simple fix
Keep only one of these files in the project source folder at a time:

- Use `src/main.cpp` for the real MOSFET sketch
- Or use `src/test.cpp` for the LED test

If you need both, rename one of them so it is not compiled, for example:

- `src/test.cpp` → [src/test_backup.cpp]
- or move it out of `src`

---

## If you want both files to coexist

Add this to `platformio.ini`:

```ini
[env:nano_r4]
platform = renesas-ra
board = nano_r4
framework = arduino
src_filter = +<main.cpp>
```

Then only `src/main.cpp` will compile.

To compile the test version instead:

```ini
src_filter = +<test.cpp>
```

---

## In plain terms

Your project is not failing because of the serial port or MATLAB; it is failing because the Arduino build has two programs in the same project.

Once you remove the duplicate / definition, the upload should proceed.

If you want, I can help you choose the correct file to keep and set up the project so both MATLAB and Arduino can communicate properly.

I’ve confirmed the build is now succeeding, and I’m comparing the two active sketches to explain the intended behavior of each one rather than just the compile status.

## What these files are meant to do

### 1) src/test.cpp
This is a simple Arduino handshake test.

It does:
- initializes serial communication at 115200
- waits for a byte from MATLAB
- checks whether that byte is `S`
- when it receives `S`, it sets `initialized = true`
- then it toggles the built-in LED every 500 microseconds

In other words, this file is just a proof that:
- MATLAB can send a command to the Arduino
- the Arduino can receive it
- the board then runs autonomously

This is a debug/test script, not the final MOSFET characterization system.

---

### 2) `src/comm.m`
This is the MATLAB side of that test.

It does:
- opens a serial port, typically COM3
- sets baud rate to 115200
- waits 2 seconds
- sends one byte: `S`
- then closes the port

This is a minimal start signal script meant to trigger the Arduino test program.

---

### 3) `src/main.cpp`
This is the real project logic that appears to be the intended characterization sketch.

It is actually a version of the test script, but it is written in a way that looks like it was meant to become the measurement system. The commented-out block at the top shows the intended behavior:

- set up serial communication
- set DAC resolution
- set ADC resolution
- output voltage sweep values
- write a voltage to DAC
- read the corresponding voltage back on ADC
- print “Applied Voltage” and “Sensed Voltage”
- loop through 0 V to 5 V in 0.1 V steps
- repeat

That means the project was aiming to do:
- generate a voltage sweep
- measure the actual sensed voltage
- print each point to the serial monitor
- eventually let MATLAB read those values and use them for MOSFET characterization

---

## So the overall intended system is:

- MATLAB sends a start command to the Arduino
- Arduino sweeps or applies voltages
- Arduino reads back voltages
- Arduino sends the data to MATLAB
- MATLAB stores/plots/analyzes the results

But the current active `src/main.cpp` has been simplified to the LED test version, so it is not yet the full characterization system.

---

## Short version

- `src/comm.m`: MATLAB start command
- src/test.cpp: Arduino test receiver + LED blink
- `src/main.cpp`: intended measurement script, but currently still simplified to the same start/LED behavior

If you want, I can rewrite `src/main.cpp` into a real working MOSFET characterization sketch and give you the matching MATLAB read code.

bool ledOn = false;
unsigned long lastToggle = 0;
const int LED_PIN = LED_BUILTIN;
const unsigned long HALF_PERIOD_US = 500;

void setRunningState(bool running)
{
    initialized = running;

    if (!running)
    {
        ledOn = false;
        digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);
    }
}

void setup()
{
    pinMode(LED_PIN, OUTPUT);
    digitalWrite(LED_PIN, LOW);

    Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop()
{
    if (Serial.available() > 0)
    {
        String command = Serial.readStringUntil('\n');
        command.trim();

        if (command.length() == 0)
        {
            return;
        }

        char cmd = command.charAt(0);

        if (cmd == 'S' || cmd == 's')
        {
            setRunningState(true);
            lastToggle = micros();
            Serial.println("START");
        }
        else if (cmd == 'O' || cmd == 'o' || cmd == '0' || cmd == 'F' || cmd == 'f' || cmd == 'X' || cmd == 'x')
        {
            setRunningState(false);
            Serial.println("OFF");
        }
        else
        {
            // Any other value turns the Arduino off.
            setRunningState(false);
            Serial.print("UNKNOWN_CMD:");
            Serial.println(command);
        }
    }

    if (initialized)
    {
        unsigned long currentTime = micros();

        if ((unsigned long)(currentTime - lastToggle) >= HALF_PERIOD_US)
        {
            lastToggle += HALF_PERIOD_US;
            ledOn = !ledOn;
            digitalWrite(LED_PIN, ledOn ? HIGH : LOW
